claims.text: Thermal treatment induces Cu segregation to grain boundaries and surfaces in FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings.
Segregated Cu forms a continuous Cu-rich phase or Cu oxide layer.
The Cu-rich layer is lubricious and improves elevated-temperature wear resistance by reducing friction and abrasive damage.
The as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating is chemically homogeneous.
The coating is a thin protective layer on a conventional metal substrate.
The intervention is annealing at approximately 600°C for 1 hour in an oxidizing atmosphere, compared with an as-deposited coating.
The proposed mechanism is applicable to wear testing between 600°C and 700°C under sliding or abrasive loading.
Annealing produces a continuous Cu-rich phase at the coating surface and along grain boundaries.
Elevated temperature promotes Cu diffusion to the surface and grain boundaries of FeNiCrCoCu.
In an oxidizing environment, segregated Cu can remain metallic or form a thin, adherent oxide.
The segregated Cu-rich phase acts as a barrier that protects the underlying high-entropy-alloy matrix from direct mechanical wear.
Annealed coatings will have lower wear rates than as-deposited coatings.
Annealed coatings will have lower friction coefficients than as-deposited coatings.
Surface analysis of annealed coatings will reveal an increased Cu-rich surface layer.
Annealed coatings will show improved microstructural integrity and less abrasive loss during high-temperature sliding.
The as-deposited baseline has no significant Cu segregation.
The proposed effect may not occur at lower temperatures or in non-oxidizing environments.
Variation in processing conditions or environmental oxygen levels may alter Cu segregation and layer stability.
Failure to obtain either a statistically significant reduction in wear or friction or an increased Cu-rich layer would falsify the hypothesis.
